Upstate NYDBER 2026: Conference Report & Consensus-Building Summary

Cornell University · June 11–12, 2026

August 07, 2026

Welcome

Upstate NYDBER 2026 brought together Discipline-Based Education Research (DBER) scholars — across Physics (PER), Biology (BER), Engineering (EER), Chemistry (CER), Geoscience (GER), and related fields — from across Upstate New York for two days at Cornell University (June 11–12, 2026). The animating question: what could this region’s DBER community build together that no single institution or field could build alone?

The conference was designed as a three-phase consensus-building process:

Phase When Focus
Before Pre-conference survey (53 responses) Hopes for the conference; top barriers & enablers to InterDBER collaboration
During Working group documents (9 small groups, both days) Naming specific barriers, bright spots, design principles, and draft InterDBER research questions
After Post-conference survey (21 responses) Conference evaluation, concrete follow-up plans, and commitments

This report synthesizes all three phases. Barriers and enablers are presented close to each group’s original language — this is intentional: Section 4 is meant to become the input for the next step in the consensus process, a community-wide rating of each barrier’s severity and changeability (and each enabler’s potential and feasibility), which has not yet been conducted.

All individual quotes and comments below are anonymized and presented as themes, not attributed to named participants.

1. Who Was in the Room

Nine small groups met throughout the conference (rotating between Working Group 1, Working Group 2, and the closing visioning session), each with 4–6 participants spanning multiple institutions, DBER fields, and career stages — from graduate students to senior faculty, across R1 universities, primarily-undergraduate institutions, and community colleges.

2. What People Came Hoping For

Pre-conference, participants described what they most hoped to get out of the conference and what they were bringing to share. Common threads:

  • Finding collaborators with complementary skills or shared interests — a recurring “who should I be looking for” theme, often phrased as wanting someone from a specific institution type (community college, R1) or with specific methodological expertise.
  • Learning how other DBER fields approach shared problems — assessment, AI in the classroom, and retention/belonging came up across many responses.
  • Bringing something concrete to the table — datasets, methods expertise, or lived experience navigating a specific institutional barrier.

3. Poster Session Gallery

Two poster sessions ran across four tracks: AI & Technology, Pedagogy & Assessment, Equity, Identity & Belonging, and Careers, Research Experiences & Curriculum/Community. Presenters gave 30-second lightning talks before each session opened, and attendees were asked to visit at least one poster from their own DBER field and one from another.

(Poster images are AI-generated conference visuals summarizing the poster session; see the conference program for the full list of presenters and titles.)

4.2 Working groups: bright spots

During Working Group 2, all nine groups discussed real collaborations that worked and what made them possible. Kept close to each group’s own language:

Cross-cutting themes that came up in multiple groups: clear/explicit communication and norm-setting; a designated convener or logistics lead; shared vision and mutual benefit; capitalizing on existing structures (centers like RIT’s CASTLE, Cornell’s CDER) that already create low-stakes, frequent cross-disciplinary contact; and in-person relationship-building as a precondition for trust.

5.2 Working groups: named barriers

Each Working Group 2 table named specific barriers and sorted them as local vs. systemic and movable vs. hard to change. This table is presented close to verbatim group language and is intended as the starting list for the post-conference severity × changeability rating round described in the conference design (see box below).

Note on Group 5: this table reported that “almost all our barriers are systemic” without naming individual items in the structured table — a useful data point in itself about how that group perceived the landscape.

Barrier landscape at a glance

5.3 Next step: the severity × changeability rating

The conference design calls for a follow-up round in which all participants rate each consolidated barrier on severity (how much does it actually block collaboration?) and changeability (how realistically can this community address it?), and each enabler on potential and feasibility. That round has not yet been conducted. 6. Design Principles for Going Forward

Each Working Group 2 table proposed 1–4 design principles for InterDBER collaboration, paired with what each would look like in practice.

Principles that surfaced independently across multiple tables: early-career and community-college inclusion, methodological pluralism, explicit/documented norms for credit and authorship, and building in space for “half-baked ideas” before they’re polished.

7. Draft InterDBER Research Questions

Working Group 1 asked each table to draft 1–3 research topics that genuinely require more than one DBER field to answer well.

Recurring topic clusters: generative AI’s impact on students and pedagogy (named by more tables than any other topic); cross-field workforce/career pathways; how disciplines differ in teaching foundational/shared content; and assessment across disciplinary contexts.

8.5 Likely follow-through

Concrete plans: several participants reported making specific follow-up plans with someone they met at the conference (see Q33/Q34 in the raw data — kept private/aggregated here since these describe named collaborations).

9. Where This Goes Next

9.1 Sustainability mechanisms people said they’d actually use

Both the post-conference survey (Q24) and the closing-session visioning tables (1–5 enthusiasm ratings per mechanism) asked what would sustain this community. Combining both sources:

Mechanism Times selected (post-survey)
Annual regional symposium 15
Slack workspace for updates and communication 13
Virtual seminar series (e.g., works-in-progress presentations) 12
Shared graduate student training or mentoring program 12
Cross-institutional reading or writing group (monthly, virtual) 9
Shared repository of instruments, protocols, and resources 8
Listserv / email list 7
Job and opportunity sharing (postings, dissertation defenses, etc.) 6
Writing retreats (in-person or virtual) 6
Network newsletter or blog for sharing works-in-progress 4
Other: 2

Highest and most consistent enthusiasm: annual regional symposium, “share and learn” seminars, and research exchange opportunities. Most divided: a network newsletter/blog and a shared digital repository — both drew high interest from some tables and low interest from others, usually tied to who would maintain them.

9.2 Three-month commitments

Participants committed to concrete next steps. Common patterns across the closing-session commitments and post-survey Q25 responses:

  • Starting or joining a journal club at their home institution
  • Connecting other DBER researchers at their institution to the network
  • Following up directly with specific people met at the conference
  • Advocating for the network with their institution’s leadership

Appendix: Data Notes

  • Pre-conference survey: 53 total responses (41 completed).
  • Post-conference survey: 21 total responses (19 completed).
  • Working group data drawn from 9 filled tables each for Working Group 1 (InterDBER research topics) and Working Group 2 (barriers, enablers, design principles), plus 9 closing-session visioning tables (sustainability ratings and commitments). A small number of tables did not fill in every field; those are reflected as gaps rather than inferred.
  • All quotes and group notes are anonymized to theme-level or group-level attribution per project guidance; no individual names appear in this report.
  • Structured source data for every table in this report lives in data/ alongside this .Rmd file, so figures and tables can be re-run or extended directly.
